turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Meera, come through. Sorry you waited, doctor was stuck on the last patient's scan on the computer.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ya, forty minutes outside. My back is killing me from that plastic chair, and I am tired of this place already.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. Sit, I'll just do your vitals. Shoes can stay.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Just do it, na. I'm twenty nine. And don't make me repeat everything, I already told the girl at the desk.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 108 over 68. Pulse 92. Oxygen saturation 99 percent. Temperature 36.7.

[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): For what it's worth, my sister was told she carries the thalassaemia trait after her delivery in Nashik. Her boy is seven now and runs around with no problem. I only say it because I have seen this in my own house.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. That's your sister. Not me.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, sorry. One second. This window has frozen again. Okay, what brings you in today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm so tired I can barely finish a day at work, and I want my blood checked.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I was on the wrong screen.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I am exhausted. I want blood tests. My husband went to a screening camp last month, they said he has thalassaemia trait. I am pregnant and both of us are having so much tension.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Camp, trait, pregnant. How many weeks are you now?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): The dating scan said eighteen weeks and two days, and that was, umm, about two weeks ago. So around twenty weeks now. First baby.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Around twenty weeks. And this tiredness, when did it start?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. I can't put a date on it. It crept up, maybe a month, maybe from the beginning, I really don't know.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dizziness? Blackouts?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Dizzy when I stand up fast, ya, a few times in a day. No blackouts. I didn't fall.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath, like you cannot finish a sentence?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I can talk. I'm snappy because I'm tired, not breathless.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever? Feeling cold, chills?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I don't feel cold.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any spotting or bleeding down below?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your bowels, your urine, any problem in either?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Both are fine. I go normally. No burning when I pass urine either.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you actually taking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Folic asid, uh, five mg, one in the morning. Not five hundred, five mg. And calcium five hundred mg at night, the antenatal clinic gave that.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every single day, the folic acid?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, most days. I miss it two or three times a week when my shift at the call centre starts early. So not the way they wrote it.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any iron? Orofer, ferrous sulphate, anything like that?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I was taking orofer, one tablet daily. I stopped it last month. My stomach was burning on it, and that settled once I left it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. I think a haemoglobin at the next antenatal visit is enough, about four weeks away. We don't need a big workup.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks? Are you even listening? The camp slip says beta thalassaemia trait, HbA2 five point two percent. Their counsellor said if I have it also, we are getting late for checking the baby.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, I saw the slip at the desk. It is the husband's HPLC, beta thal trait, HbA2 5.2 percent. Not her report.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ah. I had it in my head as a simple low haemoglobin from a camp. Say the number once more?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Five point two. HbA2. I am not saying it a third time.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five point two, got it. If you also carry the trait, two faulty haemoglobin genes can pass to the baby and the body cannot make enough healthy red blood, which is how thalassaemia major happens. Your husband's trait only makes his red cells a bit smaller, he is not ill from it. The washed-out feeling in you is mostly the pregnancy pushing your blood volume up while the baby takes the iron, not me diagnosing a disease in you.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I have it or not? Plain words.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I cannot say you have the trait. Working impression, the tiredness is from the pregnancy itself. Carrier status in you is still possible, we have not ruled it out. That is not a diagnosis.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Then kindly book the test. I took half-day leave for this only.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, the plan changes. I will book a full blood count, a ferritin, and HPLC with haemoglobin electrophoresis, this week, not in four weeks. And I am referring you to genetic counselling, that appointment will be arranged, not maybe later.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the orofer? My mother keeps saying start it again.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, do not restart the orofer. We will hold the iron till the ferritin and the HPLC come. Kindly continue the folic acid and the calcium as you are taking them.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me just look. Conjunctiva is not pale. Abdomen is soft, no tenderness. Uterus is at the umbilicus, that fits about twenty weeks.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): He gets tired too, my husband, after his night shifts. Is that the trait thing?
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Could be the trait, could be the shifts. We are not treating him today. You are the one we test.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I cannot come tomorrow morning, I have a shift. And the canteen downstairs didn't even have ginger tea, I'm just saying.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I can book Thursday with the blood room, doctor, if you sign the forms.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thursday, yes. Not fasting. Full blood count, ferritin, and HPLC. The desk will book it.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): And after that?

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back to me in two weeks with the reports, whether or not you have seen the genetics people. If you are also a carrier, the counselling will already be going on about testing the pregnancy. If you are not a carrier, the baby cannot get thalassaemia major from the two of you. Either way I want you here in two weeks.

spec.situation: Couple, wife pregnant, husband found to carry thalassaemia trait at a camp; both anxious; blood tests for the wife planned; genetic counselling discussed.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
